blocks.text: builds itself a chamber of mud for a house, that is, constructs its nest with the greatest skill. Since the ancients, Aristotle, Pliny, Plutarch and Aelian, extol this skill of the swallow with so much praise, it is surprising that they kept such deep silence about the structure of the stork's nest, which shows no less industry in this respect. Hence Alkazuinius says of the leklek, or stork: فياتي بالاعواد والحشيش وتركب بعضها في بعض تركيبا عجيبا [fa-yaʾtī bi-l-aʿwād wa-l-ḥashīsh wa-tarkab baʿḍahā fī baʿḍ tarkīban ʿajīban] It brings sticks and grasses, which it fits together in a marvellous structure. And Caspar Heldelinus, in his Encomium Ciconiae, who treats the subject most carefully: Immediately upon its first arrival the stork returns to its old nest. If it finds it safe and intact, it at once cleans it of the filth gathered during the winter neglect and restores it; but if it sees that it has been thrown down by some fiercer storm of winds, it straightway carries in twigs from the fields and marsh sedge and takes possession of the site with a new nest. First it lays out round boundaries very like a sundial; soon it builds; then it makes it firm. Finally, if anything sticks out too crookedly, it puts it in order with a wonderful industry of its beak. Moreover, they mostly build their nest on the tops of towers or on the gables of houses. Yet this is not invariable, for there are some that prefer to live in the fields. Hence Varro, Res Rusticae, book 3, chapter 5: Migrant birds rear their young, storks in the field, swallows under the roof. The nest of the field stork is in the branches of trees. Hence Olympiodorus on Job: Οὐ γὰρ εἰς γῆν τίκτει ὁ πελαργὸς, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς τὰ ὑψηλὰ τῶν δένδρων· [Ou gar eis gēn tiktei ho pelargos, all᾽ eis ta hypsēla tōn dendrōn] For the stork lays its eggs not on the ground but in lofty trees. And Alkazuinius: ولا يتخذ الوكرا الا في موضع عال كمنارة وشجرة [wa-lā yattakhidh al-wakrā illā fī mawḍiʿ ʿāl ka-manāra wa-shajara] Nor does it take a nest for itself except in a high place, for instance on a lighthouse or in a tree. And Heldelinus: It nests on the higher gables of houses, or, more rarely, in dry trees nearby. This the stork has in common with the heron: though a water bird, it nests in high places. Gesner: Although the heron seeks its food in the waters, it places its nest in woods and tall trees. Polydore Vergil, Anglica Historia, book 1: The heron is accustomed afterwards to nest in crows' nests, that is, in the tops of trees, as he adds a little later. David, however, uses firs, and a little before the cedars of Lebanon, for any tall tree, just as he uses stork for any bird that nests in a tree. The cedars of Lebanon, (he says) which he [III, 91] planted, that the birds may nest there; and the house of the stork, the firs. Although I do not in the least doubt that storks are frequent on Lebanon itself, as on the other mountain of Syria, Amanus, of which Belon says: The storks which are in Europe in summer spend a large part of the winter, as in Egypt, so also around Antioch and near Mount Amanus.

IV. The fourth passage is Ierem. VIII, 7. Even the hasida in the heaven knows her times, that is, when she must migrate from one place to another, and what the time is for departing or returning. This fits the stork as well as the rest that has been adduced. [col. 331] For it is well known that the stork is a migratory bird. And the Philosopher is objected in vain, who says that it φωλεῖν [phōlein], that is, lies hidden: Φωλεῖ, he says, ^{d)} καὶ πελαργὸς, καὶ κόττυφος, καὶ τρυγὼν, καὶ κόρυδος [Phōlei kai pelargos, kai kottyphos, kai trygōn, kai korydos]. The stork too lies hidden, and the blackbird, and the turtledove, and the lark. For that the stork withdraws and migrates to other places is taught by four kinds of witnesses. I. Greek and Roman writers. Petronius, quoting Publius:
Exile of winter, herald of the warm season.
